title: Managing Payments Across Multiple Branches: A Guide for Multi-Location Businesses
summary: Learn how multi-location payments work, from settling each branch separately to reconciling every outlet from one dashboard.
body_markdown:
Opening a new branch is a sign of growth. It also adds another set of payments for the finance team to track. Each outlet takes cards, e-wallets, QR codes, and bank transfers, and every one of those payments has to be matched to the right location before the books can close.


The volume keeps rising. In Indonesia alone, 41 million merchants accepted QRIS payments in the third quarter of 2025, and


[QRIS transaction volume grew 147.7% year on year to 4.28 billion](https://databoks.katadata.co.id/en/finance/statistics/6944c027919cc/the-number-of-qris-users-increased-in-q3-2025) , according to the Indonesian Payment System Association. For a chain with dozens or hundreds of outlets, that growth turns into a reconciliation problem.


This guide explains how multi-location payments work, the trade-offs between centralized and per-branch setups, and how to reconcile every outlet without losing visibility at either level.


Key takeaways


- Multi-location payments get harder because every branch adds payment volume, reconciliation work, and reporting needs.


- A single shared account is simple to set up but hides branch performance, while fully separate accounts fragment the books.


- The most practical setup gives each branch its own balance under one master account, with consolidated reporting at headquarters.


- Per-branch settlement and centralized reconciliation can work together when both run from the same system.


## Why multi-location payments get complicated


A single store has one cash drawer, one set of payment terminals, and one bank account. A chain with fifty outlets has fifty versions of each, and headquarters needs to see all of them clearly. Four challenges show up as the number of locations grows:


- Attribution.


Every payment has to be tied to the branch that earned it. When online orders, delivery apps, and in-store payments land in one account, finance teams spend hours working out which outlet each transaction belongs to.


- Reconciliation.


Matching payments to fulfilled orders across many outlets takes longer each month, and small mismatches add up quickly.


- Branch visibility.


Branch managers need their own sales data to run their outlets, but they should not see every other location's numbers.


- Settlement.


Some businesses want each branch to receive its own funds, while others want all money pooled at headquarters. The payment setup has to support whichever model the business chooses.


None of these problems is unique to large enterprises. A franchise with ten outlets feels the same pressure once its finance team is matching payments by hand at the end of every month.


## **Centralized vs. per-branch payment setups**


Multi-location businesses usually choose between pooling all payments or separating them completely. Each approach solves one problem and creates another.


**One shared account**


**Separate accounts per branch**


**Sub-accounts under one master account**


How it works


Every branch pays into a single account


Each branch has its own, unconnected account


Each branch has its own balance, linked to headquarters


Branch visibility


Low, since sales mix together


High for each branch


High for each branch


Headquarters visibility


High, but hard to break down


Low, since data sits in many places


High, with one consolidated view


Reconciliation


Manual sorting by branch


Repeated for every account


Automatic, by branch and in total


Best for


Very small chains


Fully independent franchisees


Growing chains and franchise networks


The third option combines the strengths of the first two. Each branch gets its own sub-account, so its payments, balance, and history stay separate. Headquarters operates the master account and sees every branch side by side. The structure works whether the business runs company-owned outlets, franchises, or both.

## **Settle each branch, reconcile from one place**


With a sub-account per branch, every payment is recorded against the outlet that earned it as soon as it arrives. That changes two things at once. Branch managers can see their own performance in real time, and headquarters no longer has to sort transactions by location at month-end.


Settlement becomes a choice rather than a constraint. A business can leave funds in each branch's balance and let outlets withdraw for local expenses. It can move money to headquarters on a schedule, or combine the two, with branches keeping a float and sending the rest to the center.


One of Xendit merchant shows how this plays out.


[Sahid Hotels & Resorts](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/sahid-hotels-resorts/) runs 26 hotel properties, each set up as a sub-account. Consolidating transaction data from every property into one dashboard reduced the manpower Sahid needs for reconciliation by 22%.


## **How to set up multi-location payments**


Moving from manual sorting to a structured setup usually follows four steps:


1. Map your locations.


List every branch, outlet, or property that takes payments, and decide which ones need their own balance.


2. Create one sub-account per branch.


Each sub-account completes business verification, then accepts payments in its own name.


3. Decide how money moves.


Choose whether branches keep their funds, sweep them to headquarters on a schedule, or do a mix of both.


4. Set up reporting at both levels.


Give branch managers access to their own data, and give finance a consolidated view across all locations.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


**What are multi-location payments?**


Multi-location payments are the payments a business collects across several branches, outlets, or properties. Managing them well means tying each payment to the location that earned it, while still giving headquarters a complete view of the business.


**Does each branch need its own bank account?**


Not necessarily. Each branch needs its own balance, so its payments and history stay separate, but funds can still be withdrawn to one company bank account. Some businesses add a separate bank account only for branches that pay local expenses.


**Can branch managers see only their own branch's data?**


Yes, if each branch has its own account. At Xendit merchant


[Sari Roti](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/sari-roti/) , each branch manager logs in to their branch's account to track its performance, while the finance team downloads reports for all branches from one dashboard.


**How do multi-location payments work for franchises?**


Franchisees usually keep their own revenue and pay the franchisor a royalty or fee. With a sub-account per franchisee, the franchisor can deduct that fee automatically using


[split rules](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) , instead of invoicing each outlet every month.


**Can a business move money from a branch to headquarters?**


Yes. On XenPlatform, the master account can move funds between sub-accounts using


[balance transfers](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transfer-balances) , for example to sweep branch revenue to headquarters at the end of each day or week.


**Does every branch have to go through business verification?**


On XenPlatform,


[verification is mandatory for every sub-account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) . The master account can submit details and documents on each branch's behalf, so branch staff do not have to handle the paperwork.
